headline: Half the extra attention a death brings is gone in about 2 days, and nine tenths within 5 days. A year later the median page still draws 1.08 times its old traffic. Award winners settle higher, a median 4.20 times, led by Nobel laureates who were barely looked up before (8.81 times).
fadeTitle: Most of the spike is gone within a week
fadeText: On the median death the page draws 206 times its usual traffic on the peak day, which is the day after the death in 44% of cases. Smoothed over a week, half the extra traffic is gone 2 days after the peak (middle half 2 to 3 days). The averaged curve loses nine tenths of its excess in 5 days and sits at 1.96 times baseline a month later and 1.09 times in the last month of the year, before jumping to 1.58 times on the anniversary. Awards lose nine tenths in 4 days, and climb again in the last week of the year as the next prize comes round.
avgAlt: Median views relative to baseline, days -60 to +365. Deaths peak at 140 times baseline and settle near 1.09; awards peak at 858 times and settle near 4.19.
curveTitle: A fast fade and a slow tail fit most events
curveText: Each event's daily views after the peak were fitted three ways, with every day counted: the baseline plus an exponential decay, plus a power law, or plus a biexponential (two exponentials, the form Candia et al. 2019 found over years in attention to songs, films and biographies). The biexponential has the lowest AIC for 76% of 1,839 deaths and 64% of 177 awards; the power law wins 14% of deaths and the exponential 9%. Where the biexponential wins, its fast part has a median time constant of 3.0 days and carries all but 1.8% of the initial excess; the slow part's median time constant is 169 days. On simulated series the selector names the true model 87% of the time for a pure exponential, 95% for a power law and 100% for a biexponential, and it calls 13% of pure exponentials biexponential, so the real share is a mild overstatement.
winsAlt: Share of events won by each model: biexponential 75%, power law 14%, exponential 11% of 2,016 events.
settleTitle: A death leaves a page a little busier than before
settleText: A year after a death the median page draws 1.08 times its old traffic, and 59% of pages sit above their baseline. Award winners settle at a median 4.20 times, but the prizes differ: Nobel laureates, with a median of 20 views a day beforehand, keep 8.81 times that; Booker winners 2.56; Ballon d'Or winners 0.87. For Academy Award winners the answer depends on which 'before' you use: against the 53 days ending a week before the nominations it is 0.58, against days -150 to -90 before the ceremony 1.03. Among deaths, each extra year of age at death goes with 2.0% less lift (p < 0.001), and pages that were busier beforehand gain less.
liftAlt: Distribution of lift. Deaths cluster near one, median 1.08; awards spread from below one to far above, median 4.20.
whoTitle: Which prize matters more than what the person did
whoText: Among deaths, the share of the first year's extra views that arrive after the first week runs from 23% (business) to 33% (writing and journalism), and median lift from 0.97 times (business) to 1.22 times (music). The gap between Nobel and Oscar winners is wider than any gap between occupations.

checksText: Bot leakage: capping any day above 50 times the median of its six neighbors touches 31 events and leaves every half-life unchanged; median lift with the cap is 1.08 for deaths and 4.20 for awards. Renames: 65 events were dropped because the article moved to a new title inside the window, and 26 articles moved later are read under the title they had at the time. Peak window: searching for the peak over days 0 to 30 instead of 0 to 3 moves it later for 163 deaths and leaves the median half-life at 2 days. Smoothing and definition: the table below gives the half-life every way it was measured. Day of week: the median page's busiest weekday draws 1.42 times its quietest, which is why every series is adjusted before measuring.
halfLifeLimit: The half-life as the spec first defined it compared a 7-day average with the single peak day, so it came out at one day for 95% of deaths. It now compares the smoothed series with its own smoothed peak (median 2 days); the old measure stays in the sensitivity table.
correction: Corrected 29 October 2026, after an independent audit. Three 2022 Nobel laureates in economics were missing because the Nobel Prize API gives the wrong year for that prize; they are now in. The curve comparison published on 28 October fitted only days above the baseline, which made a biexponential win almost by default (it reported 90%); every day now counts, and the selector was checked on simulated data. The half-life compared a smoothed series with a single raw day; it now compares like with like. 65 deaths reported days late are counted as delayed spikes rather than no spike. The Oscar baseline fell after the nominations; it now ends a week before them. Earlier figures are kept as sensitivity rows.
readmeResults:
- Peak: on the median death a page draws 206 times its baseline at the peak (middle half 115 to 395 times).
- Half-life: half the extra traffic is gone 2 days after the peak for deaths (median; 7-day smoothing against the smoothed peak) and 2 days for awards.
- Spikes: 1,839 deaths spike on days 0 to 3, 65 spike later because the news came late, 1 not at all.
- Curve shape: with every day counted, the biexponential has the lowest AIC for 76% of deaths and 64% of awards. In simulation the selector recovers the true model 87% (exponential), 95% (power law) and 100% (biexponential) of the time.
- Lift a year later: 1.08 times baseline for deaths (59% above 1), 4.20 for awards (8.81 for Nobel laureates; 0.58 for Academy Award winners against a pre-nomination baseline).
- Among deaths, each extra year of age at death goes with 2.0% less lift (p < 0.001).
- Corrected on 29 October 2026 after an audit; see the corrections note in [writeup.md](writeup.md) and entries 26 to 33 of [docs/decisions.md](docs/decisions.md).
writeupResults:
### The fade

On the median death the page draws 206 times its usual traffic on the peak day, which is the day after the death in 44% of cases. Smoothed over a week, half the extra traffic is gone 2 days after the peak (middle half 2 to 3 days). The averaged curve loses nine tenths of its excess in 5 days and sits at 1.96 times baseline a month later and 1.09 times in the last month of the year, before jumping to 1.58 times on the anniversary. Awards lose nine tenths in 4 days, and climb again in the last week of the year as the next prize comes round. 1,839 of 1,905 deaths have a visible spike (peak at least twice the baseline) on days 0 to 3. Another 65 (3.4%) have a delayed spike: nothing on days 0 to 3, then a day above twice the baseline on days 4 to 30 (Leonard Cohen, Sam Shepard and Steve Ditko among them), most often because the death became news days or weeks after it happened. 1 death has no spike at all.

### The curve

Each event's daily views after the peak were fitted three ways, with every day counted: the baseline plus an exponential decay, plus a power law, or plus a biexponential (two exponentials, the form Candia et al. 2019 found over years in attention to songs, films and biographies). The biexponential has the lowest AIC for 76% of 1,839 deaths and 64% of 177 awards; the power law wins 14% of deaths and the exponential 9%. Where the biexponential wins, its fast part has a median time constant of 3.0 days and carries all but 1.8% of the initial excess; the slow part's median time constant is 169 days. On simulated series the selector names the true model 87% of the time for a pure exponential, 95% for a power law and 100% for a biexponential, and it calls 13% of pure exponentials biexponential, so the real share is a mild overstatement. The model comparison first published on 28 October dropped every day at or below the baseline before fitting; on the same simulations that method called 100% of pure exponentials biexponential, which is why it reported 90% biexponential wins.

### The aftermath

A year after a death the median page draws 1.08 times its old traffic, and 59% of pages sit above their baseline. Award winners settle at a median 4.20 times, but the prizes differ: Nobel laureates, with a median of 20 views a day beforehand, keep 8.81 times that; Booker winners 2.56; Ballon d'Or winners 0.87. For Academy Award winners the answer depends on which 'before' you use: against the 53 days ending a week before the nominations it is 0.58, against days -150 to -90 before the ceremony 1.03. Among deaths, each extra year of age at death goes with 2.0% less lift (p < 0.001), and pages that were busier beforehand gain less.

A regression of log lift on event type, log baseline, occupation group and year (OLS, HC3 errors, n = 2,083, R² = 0.28) puts awards 194% above deaths at the same prior traffic (p < 0.001); with the Oscar baseline as the spec defined it the figure is 167% above (p < 0.001). Among deaths, with age added (n = 1,902, R² = 0.33), each extra year of age at death goes with 2.0% less lift (p < 0.001). The same regression for log half-life explains little (R² = 0.09).

### Who lasts

Among deaths, the share of the first year's extra views that arrive after the first week runs from 23% (business) to 33% (writing and journalism), and median lift from 0.97 times (business) to 1.22 times (music). The gap between Nobel and Oscar winners is wider than any gap between occupations.
